result: The KinCon reporter system can track kinase activity conformations at expression levels far below endogenous kinase levels. Specifically, BRAF-V600E was converted to a more closed conformation by PLX8394 treatment at reporter expression levels below immunoblotting detection limits.
evaluation: Claims C36 and C37 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-G demonstrating that the KinCon reporter functions at very low expression levels. The data shows dose-dependent conformational changes upon drug exposure even when reporter expression is below detection by western blot, validating the high sensitivity of the system.

result: Formation of the LKB1-STRADα-MO25 trimeric complex induces conformational changes in both LKB1 and STRADα that correlate with kinase activation. STRADα transitions from an open to a closed conformation upon complex formation, with a >10-fold increase in bioluminescence signal. Co-expression of STRADα and MO25 produces the highest increase in AMPK phosphorylation.
evaluation: Claims C38-C50 and C54 are well-supported by experimental data in Figures 2D-F showing AMPK phosphorylation increases and KinCon reporter signal changes upon co-expression of complex components. The data demonstrates that trimeric complex formation alters kinase conformations in a manner consistent with activation, though some mechanistic details (C39-C40) are stated as assumptions rather than directly demonstrated.

result: The STRADα H231A/F233A double mutation, which prevents LKB1-STRADα complex formation, abolishes the conformational changes observed in the LKB1 KinCon reporter upon trimeric complex formation.
evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2G showing that the HF mutation prevents the increase in LKB1 KinCon signal observed with wild-type STRADα. This validates that the conformational changes are dependent on protein-protein interactions at the binding interface, consistent with prior structural studies cited.

result: Among LKB1 mutations tested (K48R, R74A, K78I, D176N, D194N, W308C), only the W308C patient mutation prevented conformational closing of LKB1 upon co-expression with STRADα and MO25. This mutation disrupts a hydrophobic cluster, reduces LKB1 stability, and diminishes catalytic activity, suggesting loss of heterotrimeric complex formation ability.
evaluation: Claims C55-C67 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2I showing differential effects of mutations on LKB1 conformation. The W308C mutation uniquely prevents complex-induced conformational changes, consistent with cited literature on its effects on stability and activity. The interpretation that catalytic site residues are less important for maintaining active conformation (C63) is reasonable given the data, though speculative elements about mechanism (C65) are appropriately qualified.

result: Unlike BRAF and MEK1 KinCon reporters where the open conformation represents the active state, the closed STRADα and LKB1 KinCon conformations represent the more active kinase states.
evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by the experimental data showing that complex formation (which activates LKB1) correlates with increased bioluminescence (closed conformation) in the KinCon reporters. This represents an important finding that the KinCon technology can report different conformational dynamics for different kinase families, though the interpretation relies on correlation with AMPK phosphorylation as a readout of LKB1 activity.

result: RIPK1 and RIPK3 KinCon reporters exhibit reduced bioluminescence upon necroptosis pathway activation (TBZ treatment), indicating a shift to a more open conformation. The RIPK1 KinCon reporter is not capable of auto-phosphorylation but can be trans-phosphorylated by active flag-tagged RIPK1.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B. The reduction in bioluminescence upon pathway activation is consistent across both RIPK kinases. The trans-phosphorylation data validates that the reporter can be incorporated into functional complexes, though the lack of auto-phosphorylation capability is a limitation that should be considered when interpreting results.

result: All RIPK1 mutations tested (kinase-dead K45A, phosphorylation mimetic S14/15/166E, phosphorylation-deficient S14/15/166A, and patient mutations D324A/E/H and C601Y) led to opening of RIPK1 conformations as measured by the KinCon reporter.
evaluation: Claims C75-C81 are supported by experimental data in Figures 3G-H showing consistent conformational opening across all mutations tested. The finding that both phosphorylation mimetic and deficient mutations cause opening is described as unexpected, suggesting these mutations may affect conformation through mechanisms beyond simple phosphorylation state. The interpretation that D324 mutations affect conformation in addition to preventing caspase cleavage (C79) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

result: Allosteric RIPK1 inhibitors (Necrostatin and GSK547) induce closing of RIPK1 conformations across all tested variants including wild-type, phosphorylation mutants, and kinase-dead forms, as indicated by increased bioluminescence.
evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3J and supplements showing that both inhibitors increase bioluminescence across all RIPK1 variants tested. The finding that inactive RIPK1 complexes are also affected by drug binding is notable. However, the speculation about scaffolding functions (C85) goes beyond what the data directly demonstrate and represents an interpretation rather than a proven mechanism.

result: The CDK6-R31C and CDK4-R24C mutations reduce binding affinity for p16INK4a as measured by PPI reporter assays, and these p16INK4a-binding deficient mutants exhibit more open conformations (decreased bioluminescence) in KinCon assays.
evaluation: Claims C94-C99 are supported by experimental data in Figures 4D-E showing reduced PPI signals for the R-to-C mutations and decreased KinCon bioluminescence for the same mutants. The structural basis for reduced binding (loss of ionic interactions, C95) is supported by structural analysis in Figure 4C. The p16INK4a P40L mutation serving as a negative control validates the reporter system.

result: Three clinically applied CDK4/6 inhibitors (Palbociclib, Ribociclib, Abemaciclib) did not induce significant conformational changes in CDK4 or CDK6 KinCon reporters with varying p16INK4a binding affinities under the tested conditions.
evaluation: Claims C100-C101 and C112 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4F showing minimal effects of CDK4/6 inhibitors on KinCon reporter conformations. This is an important negative result suggesting that type I inhibitors binding to the active kinase may not induce detectable conformational changes in this system, or that the cellular context and regulatory protein interactions dominate the conformational state. The qualification 'in the tested cell culture settings' is appropriate.

result: Type I 1/2 and type III inhibitors alter KinCon conformations, while type I inhibitors do not. BRAF and MEK1 inhibitors affect active kinase conformations, RIPK1 allosteric inhibitors close both active and inactive conformations, and reducing p16INK4a binding opens CDK6 conformations.
evaluation: Claims C106-C111 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5A-C summarizing the differential effects of inhibitor types across multiple kinases. The pattern that type I inhibitors (like CDK4/6i) don't alter conformations while type I 1/2 and type III inhibitors do is consistent across the tested kinases. The interpretation about inactive RIPK1 complexes being drug targets (C110) is reasonable but somewhat speculative regarding functional consequences.

result: Similar to CDK6, PKA catalytic subunit (PKAc) conformations are primarily controlled by regulatory protein interactions. The L206R mutation, which reduces regulatory subunit binding, causes PKAc to adopt an open conformation. Forskolin treatment, which elevates cAMP and disrupts regulatory interactions, produces similar conformational opening.
evaluation: Claims C113-C119 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5D showing that the L206R mutant exhibits an open conformation and that Forskolin treatment induces similar changes. The conclusion that binary protein interactions are prime factors for altering CDK4/6 and PKAc conformations (C119) is reasonable based on the data, though it represents an inference from the experimental observations rather than a directly demonstrated mechanism.

result: The KinCon reporter system cannot track alterations in subcellular localization (cytoplasmic vs. nuclear) of kinases, as demonstrated with PKAc and BRAF reporters. The L206R mutation in PKAc did not change subcellular localization.
evaluation: Claims C120-C121 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing similar cytoplasmic and nuclear distributions for wild-type and mutant reporters. This is an important limitation of the technology to acknowledge, as it indicates the bioluminescence readout reflects conformational changes rather than localization changes.

result: The KinCon reporter technology has key advantages including robustness at varying expression levels and ability to track kinase conformations at physiologically relevant low expression levels. However, subcellular analyses and cell sorting remain challenging due to low light emission compared to fluorescence-based reporters.
evaluation: Claims C135-C137 are supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript showing function at low expression levels (Figure 1) and by the acknowledgment of technical limitations. The statement about tracking at low expression levels being important for understanding cellular functions (C137) is well-justified given that many regulatory interactions occur at physiological expression levels.

result: The manuscript provides background on kinase biology, including that the human kinome contains >500 genes encoding kinases with conserved phosphotransferase domains that regulate cellular functions through phosphorylation. Kinases act as molecular switches with ON/OFF states regulated by PTMs, scaffolding functions, protein interactions, expression patterns, and small molecules. Kinase deregulation is associated with various diseases.
evaluation: Claims C1-C17 represent well-established background knowledge about kinase biology, all supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims provide context for the study but do not represent novel findings from this work.

result: LKB1 functions as a trimeric cytoplasmic complex that regulates AMPK through phosphorylation. Mutations in LKB1 cause Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and are frequently observed in various cancers including NSCLC, cervical carcinoma, and melanoma.
evaluation: Claims C18-C22 represent established background knowledge about LKB1 biology and disease associations, supported by appropriate literature citations. These provide context for studying LKB1 with the KinCon technology.

result: RIPK1 acts as a central stress sensor controlling cell survival, inflammation, and cell death. Deregulation of RIPK1/RIPK3 signaling is linked to inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases. RIPK1/RIPK3 may share mechanistic similarities with BRAF including kinase domain dimerization and auto-phosphorylation as regulatory elements.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 represent established background knowledge about RIPK1/RIPK3 biology supported by appropriate citations. The comparison to BRAF (C25-C26) provides rationale for studying these kinases with the KinCon technology.

result: CDK4/6 regulate cell cycle progression through Rb phosphorylation. Their activity is controlled by regulatory proteins including p16INK4a (inhibitory) and cyclinD (activating). CDK4/6 inhibitors are used clinically for breast cancer, but drug resistance development necessitates personalized treatment approaches.
evaluation: Claims C27-C34 represent established background knowledge about CDK4/6 biology and clinical applications, supported by appropriate citations. These provide context for studying CDK4/6 regulation with the KinCon technology.

result: Conventional methods have limitations in capturing kinase dynamics in native cellular environments. Only a limited number of kinases are targeted by approved drugs, and many lack suitable research tools. The KinCon technology offers an innovative solution for understanding kinase conformations and could enable new intervention strategies for understudied kinases in the 'dark kinome.'
evaluation: Claims C35 and C122-C134 represent the rationale and potential impact of the KinCon technology. The limitations of conventional methods and gaps in kinase drug development are supported by appropriate citations. The statements about KinCon's potential (C126-C127, C132-C134) are reasonable inferences from the demonstrated capabilities, though they represent future possibilities rather than proven outcomes.

result: Identifying activator molecules for the LKB1-AMPK axis is more challenging than finding kinase blockers. Pseudokinases like STRADα are more than inert scaffolds and can allosterically modulate interacting kinases through switch-like transitions. There is growing interest in therapeutically restoring mutated LKB1 function.
evaluation: Claims C138-C141 provide context for the LKB1 studies and are supported by appropriate citations. The statement about pseudokinases (C139-C140) is particularly relevant given the STRADα findings in this study.

result: RIPK1 genetic alterations are linked to immune and inflammatory diseases. Small molecule inhibition of RIPK1 can counteract necroptosis in disease models. RIPK1 functions as a molecular scaffold in NFκB signaling and forms signalosomes with RIPK3. Additional kinases control RIPK1 phosphorylation and activity.
evaluation: Claims C69-C70 and C142-C146 provide additional background on RIPK1 biology and regulation, supported by appropriate citations. The comparison of K45 in RIPK1 to K78 in LKB1 (C145) is a reasonable structural observation.

result: CDK4/6 exhibit proto-oncogenic properties dependent on regulatory protein interactions. CDK6 also functions as a transcriptional regulator. The CDK4/6-cyclinD complex is hyperactivated in many cancers. CDK4/6 inhibitors are used clinically but face drug resistance challenges, necessitating precision medicine approaches.
evaluation: Claims C86-C93 provide additional background on CDK4/6 biology and clinical applications, all supported by appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for studying CDK4/6 regulatory interactions.

result: Kinase inhibitors are classified by the activation state they bind: Type I inhibitors bind active conformations (DFG in, αC in), Type I 1/2 bind inactive states (DFG in, αC out), Type II bind inactive kinases (DFG out), and Type III (allosteric) inhibitors bind adjacent to the ATP pocket allowing simultaneous ATP binding.
evaluation: Claims C102-C105 represent established knowledge about kinase inhibitor classification, supported by appropriate citations. This classification framework is used to interpret the differential effects of inhibitors on KinCon conformations.

result: In silico predictions suggest that more than 200 protein kinases contain cis-regulatory elements, many of which act as auto-inhibitory modules (AIMs).
evaluation: Claims C147-C148 are supported by citations to prior work including the authors' own studies. This provides context for the broader applicability of the KinCon technology to kinases with auto-inhibitory mechanisms.
